module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 72

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/72](https://www.erdosproblems.com/72)
- [Er94b] Erdős, Paul, *Some problems in number theory, combinatorics and combinatorial geometry*.
  Math. Pannon. (1994), 261-269.
- [Er95] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite problems in number theory, combinatorics, and
  geometry*. Resenhas (1995), 165-186.
- [Er97b] Erdős, Paul, *Some old and new problems in various branches of combinatorics*. Discrete
  Math. (1997), 227-231.
- [Er97c] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favorite problems and results*. The mathematics of Paul
  Erdős, I (1997), 47-67.
- [Bo77] Bollobás, Béla, *Cycles modulo $k$*. Bull. London Math. Soc. (1977), 97-98.
- [Ve05] Verstraete, Jacques, *Unavoidable cycle lengths in graphs*. J. Graph Theory (2005),
  151-167.
- [LiMo20] Liu, Hong and Montgomery, Richard, *A solution to Erdős and Hajnal's odd cycle
  problem*. arXiv:2010.15802 (2020).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter SimpleGraph

namespace Erdos72

open scoped Classical in
/--
Is there a set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ of density $0$ and a constant $c>0$ such that every graph on
sufficiently many vertices with average degree $\geq c$ contains a cycle whose length is in $A$?

Bollobás [Bo77] proved that such a $c$ does exist if $A$ is an infinite arithmetic progression
containing even numbers (see [71](https://www.erdosproblems.com/71)).

Erdős was 'almost certain' that if $A$ is the set of powers of $2$ then no such $c$ exists
(although he conjectured that $n$ vertices and average degree $\gg (\log n)^{C}$ suffices for
some $C=O(1)$). If $A$ is the set of squares (or the set of $p\pm 1$ for $p$ prime) then he had
no guess.

Solved by Verstraëte [Ve05], who gave a non-constructive proof that such a set $A$ exists.

Liu and Montgomery [LiMo20] proved that in fact this is true when $A$ is the set of powers of $2$
(more generally any set of even numbers which doesn't grow too quickly) - in particular this
contradicts the previous belief of Erdős.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos72.lean#L184"]
theorem erdos_72 : answer(True) ↔ ∃ A : Set ℕ, A.HasDensity 0 ∧ ∃ c : ℚ, 0 < c ∧
    ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), c ≤ G.averageDegree →
      ∃ (v : Fin n) (w : G.Walk v v), w.IsCycle ∧ w.length ∈ A := by
  sorry

open scoped Classical in
/--
Liu and Montgomery [LiMo20] proved that there is a constant $c > 0$ such that every graph on
sufficiently many vertices with average degree $\geq c$ contains a cycle whose length is a power
of $2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos72.lean#L157"]
theorem erdos_72.variants.powers_of_two : ∃ c : ℚ, 0 < c ∧
    ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop, ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), c ≤ G.averageDegree →
      ∃ (v : Fin n) (w : G.Walk v v), w.IsCycle ∧ ∃ k : ℕ, w.length = 2 ^ k := by
  sorry

end Erdos72

reformulations.difference: The source asks for 'a constant c > 0' (a real constant) and the average degree is the real number 2|E|/n (UCSD version: 'c(A)n edges'). The Lean takes c : ℚ and uses the repository's ℚ-valued `SimpleGraph.averageDegree` = (∑_v deg v)/n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: By the handshake lemma ∑_v deg v = 2|E|, so the ℚ-valued average degree cast to ℝ equals 2|E|/n. The property 'every G with c ≤ avg(G) has a cycle with length in A' is monotone in c, so a real witness c > 0 can be replaced by any rational q ≥ c with q > 0 (exists_rat_gt), and every rational witness is a real witness. In a scratch file I proved, for an arbitrary conclusion predicate Q, (∃ c : ℚ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ᶠ n, ∀ G, c ≤ G.averageDegree → Q n G) ↔ (∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ᶠ n, ∀ G, c ≤ 2|E(G)|/n → Q n G). This is also exactly the gap between this statement and the real-valued statement proved in the linked plby/lean-proofs file.

reformulations.difference: Liu–Montgomery (arXiv 2010.15802, Cor. 1.3 and the remark after it) prove that EVERY graph with average degree ≥ d has a cycle whose length is a power of 2, with no threshold on the number of vertices. The Lean asks this only for graphs on sufficiently many vertices (`∀ᶠ n in atTop`), with rational c. It also allows 2^0 = 1 and 2^1 = 2, which no cycle length can equal.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: 'Every graph' implies 'eventually' trivially. Conversely, suppose the eventual version holds with threshold N, and let H be a graph on m ≥ 1 vertices with avg(H) ≥ c (m = 0 is vacuous, since averageDegree = 0 < c there). Take the disjoint union of k copies of H with km ≥ N. It has the same average degree, and each of its cycles is connected, so it lies in a single copy and is a cycle of H of the same length. Relabelling onto Fin (km) changes neither the average degree nor the cycle lengths. So the eventual version implies the version for all graphs. The ℚ-versus-ℝ choice of c is harmless by the monotonicity argument proved in Lean for erdos_72. The spurious lengths 1 and 2 never occur, since IsCycle forces length ≥ 3. I proved only the ℚ/ℝ part in Lean, not the disjoint-union step.

review.notes:
Both declarations state the source's claims faithfully, and category, answer and formal_proof records are consistent with erdosproblems.com ('PROVED – solved in the affirmative'). Lean checks, all in /workspace/review:
(1) equiv.lean proves that rational c with ℚ `averageDegree` is equivalent to real c with 2|E|/n. It also proves averageDegree = 0 on Fin 0 and that the empty graph has no cycle, which is why `0 < c` is forced and harmless.
(2) sanity.lean checks that averageDegree(K₃) = 2 and that K₃ has an `IsCycle` walk of length 3.
The `∀ᶠ n` ('sufficiently many vertices') in erdos_72 is in the source itself, both on erdosproblems.com and in the UCSD entry ('for n > n₀(A)'). By the disjoint-union argument it is equivalent to Verstraëte's 'every graph' form. The linked plby/lean-proofs statements use `c : ℝ`, a real average degree 2|E|/n and `∃ N₀, ∀ n ≥ N₀`. They define `Set.HasDensity` the same way as this repository, so they are equivalent to the statements here, and the line anchors (L184, L157) point to the right theorems. I did not check that the external proof's large Erdos63/Liu–Montgomery dependency tree is free of sorry and axioms. That affects only how much the formal_proof record can be trusted, not whether the statements are faithful.
